To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

photochemically induced dynamic polarization of 1H, 13C, and 15N nuclei can be used to study the conformation of the proteinase and inhibitor molecules in solution and in their proteinase–inhibit complex, as well as the interactions between the proteinase and the inhibitor.
the accessibility of surface aromatic amino acids in the proteinase and in the inhibitor is lost on complex formation, and that this loss is more pronounced in the proteinase than in the inhibitor.

the accessibility of surface aromatic residues in proteinases and protein inhibitors can be used to probe proteinase–inhabitor complexation, that the complexation site is located at or close to the surface of the proteinase, and that the complexation process involves a change in the proteinase structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of proteinase–inhibition complexes by the use of photochemically induced dynamic polarization (CIDNP) of nuclear spin magnetization.
the study of the accessibility of surface aromatic residues in proteins and protein complexes.
the study of protein–protein interactions by means of a novel photochemical probe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the accessibility loss in the proteinase is due to a conformational change, and the loss in the inhibitor due to the binding of the proteinase to the inhibitor.
photo‐CIDNP is a very useful method in the study of protein–protein interactions, but it has its limitations, and it should be used with care.

photo‐CIDNP is an extremely useful technique to study the accessibility and the dynamics of protein residues, in solution, and that the technique can be used to study interactions in the proteinase‐proteinase inhibitor complexes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surface residues in proteinases and their inhibitors are not rigidly fixed, but are mobile, and that the mobility of surface residues is reduced upon complex formation.

the proteinase–proteinase inhibitor complex is more compact than the individual proteins, and that there is an interaction between the proteinase and the inhibitor which extends over the entire surface of the proteins.

the photochemically induced accessibility loss of the surface aromatic residues in the proteinase and inhibitor is a sensitive probe for the proteinase–protein inhibitor contact site and that the proteinase–protease inhibitor interaction is accompanied by the formation of a new structure, which may be a precursor of the final complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
photochemically induced dynamic polarization can be used to study protein–protein interactions.
the accessibility of surface residues is a useful probe of protein–protein complex formation, even in the absence of structural information.
photochemically induced dynamic polarizations are sensitive probes for the study of protein–protein interactions.
